before.rappels: 2 rappels down slabs north of the exit gully (one party used two 30m ropes), plus a protected wet-ledge traverse

rappel_detail.anchor: Natural, and not guaranteed to be in place — you may need to rig the anchor yourself, and one earlier party describes rappelling from a slung tree on the southeast-facing ledge. Carry webbing and nuts for this descent.
hazards: No reliable fixed station — arriving expecting one and finding nothing is the failure mode here
You are committing off the summit onto a face on the opposite side of the peak from the couloir you climbed
rappel_detail.station: From the summit, descend back to the upper rock band; the single rappel from there drops onto the ledge on the southeast face.

rappel_detail.anchor: Natural / rigged; an older two-rope description used a stopper anchor part way up the southeast face.
hazards: Anchors may have to be built from nuts and left behind
rappel_detail.station: First of the rappels down the gully lying east of the top of the Northeast Couloir, entered from the southeast-face ledge.

rappel_detail.notes: A third rappel in this gully is described as sometimes necessary, so treat the count as two or three here rather than fixed.
hazards: Loose gully; the transition onto snow at the bottom may need axe and crampons depending on season
rappel_detail.station: Continues down the same gully; the sequence ends on the snow slopes below, from which parties traverse toward the Colchuck-Dragontail notch or glissade the Colchuck Glacier.

access.notes: Day-use permit: free, self-issue at trailhead, required May 15-October 31. Overnight: an Alpine Lakes Wilderness Enchantments overnight permit is required June 15-October 15 (limited availability, application-based). Parking is $5 per vehicle per day (or $30 annual Northwest Forest Pass), at the Stuart Lake Trailhead parking lot, right side of FR 7601 only. Forest Road 7601 typically closed November to May; recommended season is June through October (climbing season May-June for snow/ice conditions). Restrictions: parking only on right side of FR 7601; no dispersed camping between FR 7601 and Icicle Creek; dogs not allowed in Alpine Lakes Wilderness; motorized equipment prohibited.
access.permit: Self-issued day-use wilderness permit at the trailhead; overnight permit required May 15-Oct 31 for camping
access.landManager: Okanogan-Wenatchee National Forest - Alpine Lakes Wilderness

access.fees: Overnight camping in this basin is inside the Enchantment Permit Area, so the paid lottery applies: $5.00 per person per day for the overnight permit, May 15 - October 31, plus a $6 non-refundable lottery application fee. There is no fee for a day climb beyond the free self-issued trailhead permit.
access.notes: Do not confuse this approach with the actual Enchantment Permit Area lottery (Stuart/Colchuck/Snow Lakes/Eightmile/Core zones, reached via the Stuart Lake or Snow Lakes trailheads) — Argonaut Peak's standard approaches are separate, non-quota Alpine Lakes Wilderness trailheads.
access.rules: Standard USFS Alpine Lakes Wilderness group-size limit of 12 (people + stock). Bear-resistant food storage mandatory forest-wide.
access.permit: Overnight camping in this basin is inside the Enchantment Permit Area's Stuart Zone and needs a quota permit obtained in advance through the Recreation.gov lottery (May 15 - October 31). Day use needs only the free self-issued permit at the trailhead.
access.closures: Beverly Creek/Fourth Creek Pass (FR-9737-112, Beverly Turnpike Trailhead) and several nearby Teanaway trails (Longs Pass, Ingalls Way, Standup Creek, etc.) were closed under a USFS order effective May 20-Dec 31, 2026 following the 2025 Labor Mountain Fire — confirm current status with the Cle Elum Ranger District before planning a Teanaway-side approach.

partner_requirements.fitnessSpec: Fit for a long, full-value day (~15.5 hrs)
requiredSkills: Real snow/ice competence — self-arrest, crampon/axe on firm 30-40°+ approach couloir terrain that can hold firm snow/ice into July
Route-finding judgment — a ledge/gendarme maze near the top is repeatedly cited as the navigation crux
Brush/bushwhack tolerance on the Mountaineer Creek approach
partner_requirements.experienceLevel: Solid 5.7-5.8 trad leader (crux can reportedly feel stiffer than 5.6)

July.reason: Early July couloir often still consolidating, may need full snow/ice kit; mid-to-late July usually melted/consolidated

June.reason: Couloir typically firm snow/ice, avalanche-adjacent, brush approach snow-covered

August.reason: Most reliably dry/consolidated, longest daylight for the long day

September.reason: Optimal early-to-mid month; late September marginal given the 15.5-hr day length versus daylight, plus early snow risk

waypoints.name: Snow-covered granite slab

waypoints.name: 40+ degree snow/ice couloir
waypoints.note: Couloir steepens to 40+ degrees near its top; crampons recommended for the final pitch to the notch.

waypoints.name: Notch below the Northwest Arete
waypoints.note: Gain the ridge here and rope up for roughly seven pitches of Class 4 to 5.6+ climbing up the arete.

waypoints.name: Argonaut Peak summit (west summit, true)
waypoints.note: True summit is the west of two nearly equal summits (SE and W); most parties reverse the arete with short rappels through the crux, then downclimb the couloir.

before.approach: From the Beverly Turnpike Trailhead (Bean Creek/Beverly Creek TH) off the North Fork Teanaway River Road (FR-9737-112), the approach is well-documented with concrete checkpoints: at about 0.5 mile, bear left onto signed Trail #1391 (Beverly Turnpike Trail) — a wrong fork onto the Bean Creek Trail here is a commonly reported mistake, so double-check the sign. At about 3.1 miles, turn right onto Trail #1226.1 (Fourth Creek Trail). At about 3.6 miles you crest Fourth Creek Pass with the first open views of Argonaut, Colchuck, and Dragontail. Continue down the far side to about 6 miles and ~4,200 ft, where you ford Ingalls Creek (wading or a footlog) to reach good flat camping at the Fourth Creek/Ingalls Creek confluence — day one is roughly 6 miles and 2,000 ft of gain. From camp, follow the Ingalls Creek Trail west for about half a mile, then cut sharply left (north) and start climbing straight upslope toward Argonaut's south face: expect brushy 'jackstraw' forest for the first 300 vertical feet and then dense slide alder for close to 1,000 feet above that (progress can slow to a few hundred feet per hour in the thick of it — stay right/climber's-right to minimize brush where possible). At about 5,200 ft the brush relents onto open slopes; ascend the left side of a large drainage gully up to about 6,600 ft, then continue up the gully itself. At about 7,100 ft the gully forks — the standard line is the left branch (the right also goes but is less traveled). Climb to the right side of the summit face and find the route's technical crux: a 50-foot gully with a chockstone near its top (Class 4 — step right at the overhang to avoid harder class 5 moves), which tops out on the east ridge; follow this a short distance to the summit. Hazards: the Ingalls Creek ford, sustained brush-bashing on the lower slopes, and possible snow in the gully in shoulder season (carry an axe/crampons if conditions warrant).

pitch_detail.notes: Start in the short left-facing corner with a crack in it and follow blocky, generally solid granite up the lower face; watch for loose blocks right at the base.

Continue up the broad face on good rock — climbers can pick their own line here since the face is featured almost anywhere — working toward the right side of the summit wall to set up for the top-out gully.

The 50-foot gully with a chockstone near its top is Class 3 until the final stepping-right move past the chockstone (step right at the overhang to dodge a harder 5th-class option); short and only Class 4, but it's the route's real crux thanks to the exposure and a heavily-worn sling anchor right above it — back it up with fresh webbing. Tops directly onto the east ridge a short walk from the summit.

before.detailed_rack: Short route — 300ft/3 pitches of blocky Class 5.6 on generally good granite directly below the summit. A single set of nuts plus cams in the 0.4-2in range (with extra pieces in the 0.75-1in range, reported as the most useful crux size) is sufficient; nothing larger is recorded as needed. Bring webbing or a cordelette specifically for building/backing up the crux-pitch anchor.
gear: webbing/cordelette for the crux belay/rap anchor
before.bail: Retreat via the same 50-ft rappel back into the gully, then downclimb class 2-4 terrain toward Ingalls Creek.

before.detailed_rack: Single set of nuts and cams from finger-size through ~3in covers the ridge's crack and corner systems; nothing larger is reported as needed. The East Ridge is most commonly encountered as the standard rappel descent off the Northwest Arete (Argonaut-Colchuck Col in 4 rappels) with established anchors found at each station, so bring cordelette/webbing to back up or replace tat if worn.
before.permit: Enchantment permit area: overnight stays May 15-Oct 31 require a quota permit (Recreation.gov advance lottery); day trips need the free self-issued day-use permit at the trailhead.
